items.label: section_header
items.text: CARBON DIOXIDE

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.7 Copper(II) carbonate decomposes to form carbon dioxide when heated.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: You should remember the colours of copper(Il) carbonate and copper(II) oxide.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: A hydrocarbon is a molecule containing carbon and hydrogen only. These are discussed more fully in Unit 4.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Non-metal oxides are covalent compounds.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Non-metal oxides are usually acidic oxides, which react with alkalis/bases to form salts.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Non-metal oxides are often soluble in water and react with it to form acidic solutions containing hydrogen (H⁺) ions.

items.label: text
items.text: Carbon dioxide is a colourless gas that is most easily made in the laboratory by the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate in the form of marble chips:

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } ( s ) + 2 H C l ( a q ) \rightarrow C a C l _ { 2 } ( a q ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: text
items.text: Carbon dioxide can also be obtained when metal carbonates are heated strongly.

items.label: text
items.text: Most carbonates split to give the metal oxide and carbon dioxide when you heat them. This is an example of thermal decomposition, breaking up something by heating it.

items.label: text
items.text: For example, copper(ll) carbonate is a green powder which decomposes on heating to produce black copper(ll) oxide:

items.label: formula
items.text: C u C O _ { 3 } ( s ) \rightarrow C u O ( s ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: Calcium carbonate doesn't decompose unless it is heated at quite high temperatures. This is a commercially important reaction because it is used to convert limestone (calcium carbonate) into quicklime (calcium oxide):

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } ( s ) \rightarrow C a O ( s ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g )

items.label: section_header
items.text: CARBON DIOXIDE AND GLOBAL WARMING: THE GREENHOUSE EFFECT

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 13.8 The greenhouse effect

items.label: text
items.text: Carbon dioxide is produced when fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) burn. For instance, when coal, which is mostly carbon, burns in excess oxygen:

items.label: formula
items.text: C ( s ) + O _ { 2 } ( g ) \rightarrow C O _ { 2 } ( g )
